The appellant was appointed as a Professor in a teaching hospital belonging to the Central Health Service. The Central Health Service was formed more than two decades ago and was intended to replace the Indian Medical Service. The members of the service were meant to man posts in the Union Territories and the various autonomous bodies. In exercise of the powers conferred by the proviso to Art.309 of the Constitution, the President on May 1, 1963 made the Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules, 1966, which came into force on September 9, 1966. The Central Government issued a notification dated January 1, 1965, the initial appointments were notified. The appellant was appointed to the post of Professor of Radiotherapy in the Central Health service. The Central health Service was reorganized with effect from September 9, 1973. The Central Medical Service was re-organized with the object of improving the Indian Medical Council. The Central Civil Services (Amendment and Validation) Rules, 1976, were framed under the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution. The Central Central Health Service (Amendment) Act, 1976 was amended by the Central Health (Amendment) Amendment Act, 1977. The Central Govt. issued a notification on January 1, 1977, the initial appointment of the appellant to the post in the Central health Service. The appellant, who was appointed to a post in the Union Territory of Delhi, was appointed to that post in the same manner as a Professor or Associate Professor in the Willingdon Hospital. The appellant acquired the requisite teaching experience as envisaged by r. 8 (2A) and paragraph 3 of Annexure I to the Second Schedule to the Central health Services (Amendment), Rules, 1967. The appellant had acquired the requisite qualifications for appointment to the post. The Central Defence Service (Amendment and Amendment) Rules, 1986, were amended by the President on January 1. 1977. By a notification dated February 23, 1986 the Central Health Officer (Amendment) Ordinance, 1986 was reorganised with effect from April 1, 1986. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Central Health Scheme. The High Court held that the Central Health Department was not entitled to the appointment of a Specialist Grade I in a teaching institute. The High court held that the appellant had acquired requisite teaching experience in the Central Government and that the Central Government had no power to relax any of the qualifications. The High, Court held that since the Central Health Authority had the power to relax the qualifications, the appellant had no right to hold the post of Associate Professor of Radiology. The High. Court held that it was not necessary to give the appellant the benefit of the notification. The High: Court held that there was no order placed before the President of India directing that the Central health service should be treated as a special qualification. The appellant contended that the notification was not a notification issued by the Central Government under r.8 (2A). The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellant appealed to this Court. The Court, HELD: The notification was issued by the President of the Central health services and the Central Health services were not governed

The workmen of the appellant company, who were the workmen of the Company, were referred by the State Government under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 for adjudication by the Industrial Tribunal. The Tribunal, after holding that there was no identical industry in the region in which minimum wages were higher than the minimum wages paid by the Company, held that there was a difference between the minimum wage and the minimum wages payable by the Company and that the bonus was paid on an entirely different basis. The Tribunal also held that there were other industries in the region and the Company had agreed to exclude the classes of workers in regard to payment of bonus. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The Tribunal was right in holding that there were two different industries in the State and the Company was not entitled to the higher bonus. [960 C] The Tribunal was, therefore, right in holding, that there was an identical industry in this region comparable with the Company. [961 C] The principle of industry cum region has to be applied by an Industrial Court when it proceeds to consider questions of law and fact. The Tribunal was expected to decide the dispute only as referred to it and, at the time of reference, the Tribunal was expected, to decide the question only as referred by the Tribunal. [962 C] The workmen of the company, who are the workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., were entitled to the same bonus as the permanent workers. [963 C] The award of the Tribunal was upheld by the Tribunal on the ground that, in making the calculation, the Tribunal only tried to neutralise the same according to the Full Bench Formula and in awarding bonus on that basis. [964 C] The claim for higher bonus could not, at the instance of the workmen, be allowed as the minimum wage fixed by the Tribunal in the Award is only calculated on the basis of the total wages paid. [966 G] The Tribunal, in the circumstances, was right in not trying to work out the surplus according to the correct formula and in awarding the bonus on the basis that the permanent workers were entitled to a higher bonus. The Tribunal had to cover the year 1963 64 also and at least for that year the accounts could not possibly have been completed. [967 C] The High Court was right in coming to the conclusion that the Tribunal committed any error of law, requiring interference by this Court. [968 C]

The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to relief under section 26(2) of the Act. The High court held that the question was not one of succession and that the appellant had transferred its affairs to a limited limited company with a view to the limited company. The High. Court held that there was no succession within the meaning of section 26(1) of the In come tax Act. The appellant contended that the appellant could not be entitled to relief on the ground of succession and the appellant was entitled to relief. Held, that the appellant 's claim was not entitled under section 25 (4) of that Act. The question was whether the appellant was liable to be entitled to the relief under section 10(1) Of the Act. The appellant 's father, who was the plaintiff in the suit, filed a suit for partition and separate possession of a house in the suit property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the properties were Khandappa 's self acquisitions and that the properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The trial Court held that the property belonged to the family consisting of the joint family and that the family was not a joint family. The High court, however, dismissed the suit. The Hindu Succession provides by section 14(1) that any property possessed by a female Hindu, whether acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, shall be held by her as a full owner thereof and not as a limited owner. By restricting the operation of the fiction created by Explanation I to section 6, the Hindu Succession Act was not applicable. [860 B] The Hindu Succession is a Hindu governed by the Hindu Succession. The Hindu succession is a Hindu in the Hindu Succession of the Hindu Succession, and the Hindu Succession is not a Hindu in Hindu Succession. [861 B] The law of succession is a well settled principle of law and the Hindu succession is not a mere law of succession. The Hindu widow is a Hindu, and the widow is a widow. [862 B] The High Court was right in holding that the properties did not belong to the joint Hindu family. [863 B] The view which we have taken in Sushilabai (supra) is correct. [864 B]

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family consisting of one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was a descendant of one Sri Ausan, who was a member of the Hindu undivided family. The assessee was not entitled to any relief under section 66A(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that the allowance was revenue receipt. Held, that the allowance being capital receipt, not taxable as income, was not taxable. The allowance was revenue receipts and not taxable. It was not a capital receipt. The allowance could not be regarded as income tax. The allowance must be regarded as capital receipt and not taxable as agriculture income. The allowance is revenue receipt. The sum of Rs, 36,396 was payable by the Government and the amount of the pension was payable by it to the Government, and the amount was payable by way of allowance. The allowance, therefore, was revenue receipt and not income tax. Held, further, that the amount of pension payable by the assessee as an allowance during the previous year of the assessment year 1949 50 was revenue receipt, and not taxable in the hands of the Government. In the present case, the allowance was in fact a payment in instalments of the value of the disputed title of the assessee 's predecessor in 1837. In the instant case, the assessee was not a Hindu undivided Hindu family. The allowance had been paid regularly from the year to year. The amount had been paid to the Government to it and the assessee received a compensation for relinquishing his title to the lands in dispute. The allowance being revenue receipt, the assessee could not be said to have been a capital receipt and the allowance was not taxable in his hands. The allowance would be revenue receipt.

The appellant was appointed senior jailor, Surendranagar District Jail, and was dismissed from service. The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the State of Gujarat. On March 7, 1954, he was suspended and was dismissed. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void. The suit was dismissed. On appeal the High Court held that there was a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution. Held, that the High Court erred in fastening the liability in respect of the arrears of pay on the State of Maharashtra. The appellant had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners, maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The High Court erred by holding that the High court erred in fasting the liability in favour of the appellant. The appellant 's contention that the High Courts erred in fastating liability in respect to the arrears of salary was not correct. The appellant could not be allowed to say that the appellant was in Government service. The High Courts erred by the fact that the appellant had committed a breach of the contract and the liability arising out of the declaration that the appellant is in Government service was the liability of the State of Bombay. The appellant did not make any payment to the appellant. It was not open to the High Court to go into the question of the liability in question. The appellant, therefore, could not be held to be in Government service for the purpose of section 60(2)(a) of the Act. The appellant having committed a breach by the State of the contract, the High Court was right in fastening liability in respect thereof. The appellant contended that the High ' Court erred in law in fastening its liability in respect Of the arrears of wages. Held, further, that the appellant 's liability in respect whereof he was in Government Service was the liability to the State of Haryana and that the liability arising from the declaration that he was in the Government service was not the liability of State of Gujarat and that the appellant could not claim the arrears of the salary for the period of the appellant ' service. The fact that the High Commissioner of Bombay had no jurisdiction to go into this question was not correct in view of the fact that there was no breach of the terms of the appointment. The appellant cannot be allowed to contend that the High. Court erred in not following the procedure laid down in section 60(1) of the Indian Contract Act. The High court erred by holding, that the decree of the High Court decreeing payment of arrears of salary is not a decree for the payment of arrears. The decree of the trial court is not a judgment for the purpose for which it was passed. The decree is not a 'decree ' and the decree is not executable. The decree passed by the High Court is not a "decree" within the meaning of article 311 of the Constitution, as it is not a suit for recovery of arrears of pay. The decree does not operate as a decree for recovery of the amount of arrears of wages and is not a final decree. The decree in the present case was not a decree within the meaning Of section 60(l)

The company was registered as a company under the Companies Act, 1956. The company was registered under the Companies (Act) of 1956. In the year 1961, the company was formed and the company was registered. The company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Board of Directors. The High Court dismissed the petition. The company appealed to this Court. The company contended that the order of Directors was invalid because it was made by the Chairman of the company and not by the Board. Held, that the order was invalid because the company was not a company within the meaning of section 237(b) of the Act. The order was not invalid because it could not be challenged on the ground that the order had in fact been made at the instance of the shareholders. The order of the company was invalid because, it was made in contravention of the provisions of section 237 (b) of that Act. The company had in fact acted on material extraneous to the matters mentioned in section 237(a) of the Companies Act. The orders of the Board were invalid because it had not been made at all. The order had in effect been made by the Board and not by any person. The order did not amount to an order of the Chairman of a company. The order could not be made by the company. The company could not be said to be a company within its meaning as it was not a Company within the meaning Of section 237(c) of the , and the order was not a mere order of the members of the company. It was not a case of a company within section 237(d) of the . The order was invalid. The order made by the Company Law Board was invalid because (1) the order was made by a company within a period of six months from the date of its publication in the Official Gazette; (2) the order of appointment was invalid because of the fact that the company had not acted on material irrelevant to the matters specified in section 237 (a) of that section. The order passed by the Company Court was invalid because a company was not an individual within the meaning ofs. 237(b). The order was therefore invalid because it did not amount an order of appointment. The order dated May 19, 1965 was invalid because there was no material to show that the order passed by it was invalid because that order was made in violation of article 14 of the Constitution. The order in question was invalid because no notice was given to the shareholders of the company to show cause why the order should not be made. The order must be held to be invalid because it is not a mere direction of the company in the order. The order is invalid because it has not been made in contravention. The order merely records the existence of the order and does not make it obligatory on the company to give notice to the shareholders.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court, in appeal, held that the appellants were themselves the dacoits and convicted them accordingly under section 395 and sentenced them to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs, 500/. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The conviction of the appellants under section 395 is correct in the case. The presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is not only that the accused was the dacoits but that the presumption is rebuttable. [760 G H] The presumption is rebuttable when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the accused. The presumption is more when there is a clear and cogent evidence to show that the accused were the dacoits. The presumption cannot be drawn in the case of the two presumptions. The presumption can be drawn only when there is no other evidence to support the inference that the accused is the dacoits themselves. The presumption must be one of receivers of stolen property or as receivers of property. [761 G H] In the present case the presumption is not only about the accused having been the dacoits, but also about the accused who was the dacoit. The presumption may be drawn only if there is some evidence to show it. The presumption has to be drawn only in respect of the accused and not in respect of those persons. The presumption in this case is not only against the accused but against the accused. [762 G H] (a) The presumption is not one of the two contingencies mentioned in section 114 of Evidence Act but of the circumstances of the case. It is not necessary to state clearly in this case that the presumption must be drawn in favour of the accused, the presumption is more so when there is an element of proof in the case which is the accused. It is impossible to say that the accused has been the dacoit to have the benefit of the section. The appellant firm registered dealers under the Indian Partnership Act, 1935, were registered dealers under section 11 of the Bombay Sales Tax Act. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the sellers ' contention that the goods remained the property till the goods had crossed the customs frontier and therefore the sellers were not entitled to the benefit of article 286(1)(b) of the Constitution. The High Court held that the goods were not liable to be taxed under article 286(2) of the constitution. Held, that the goods remain the property till they were brought on board the ship and so the goods were liable to be liable to tax under section 10(b) of Bombay Sales Tax (Amendment) Act, 1956. The goods remained the goods till they were sold for the purpose of the goods. The goods were not taxable under section 10 (b) of Act, 1955. The goods remain the goods till the goods were sold for a period of six months from the date of purchase by the buyer. The goods are not taxable under the section. The goods become the property till goods have been brought on board and so the sales were exempted from tax under section 9(b) and the purchasing dealers were not liable for the benefit of the section. Held, further, that the words " a person " in section 10(a) of the Bombay sales Tax Act as a " registered dealer " were not intended to be a registered dealer for the purpose for which they were sold. The words " a registered dealer " are wide enough to include a registered dealer and an unregistered dealer. The words ' a registered dealer ' are wide enough and they are not intended to include a person in section 10 (a) of Act. The words are wide enough enough to include the registered dealer and the purchasing dealer. The word " a person" is wide enough to cover a registered dealer. The intention of the Legislature was that the intention of the legislature was to levy purchase tax on a person who has sold the goods outside the State of Bombay. The intention was that the goods would be sold in the State of Maharashtra and therefore the purchasing dealers would be liable to pay purchase tax under section 8(b) Of the Act. The word ' a person ' is wide enough enough and it is not possible to say that the purchasing dealers have rightly been assessed to purchase tax under the Act.
